routes.description: Establish a cumulative body of historical facts concerning burial, the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the origin of resurrection belief, then show that bodily resurrection may be considered historically and explains those facts better than competing accounts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the core facts are sufficiently established, the inference to divine bodily resurrection is methodologically admissible, and that hypothesis has greater comparative explanatory adequacy than the relevant naturalistic or rival theological alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus' bodily resurrection is the best explanation of the historically established aftermath of the crucifixion.

centralBridges.description: Establish the burial, empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and emergence of sincere resurrection belief as facts requiring a unified explanation.
Show that historical reasoning may compare a divine-resurrection hypothesis with alternatives without excluding it solely because it invokes supernatural agency.
Demonstrate that resurrection accounts for the relevant facts with stronger explanatory scope, fit, and plausibility than the competing hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the adequacy of early traditions and central narrative agreement despite disputed authorship, transmission, interests, and differences in detail.
Use Jewish bodily-resurrection concepts and Jesus' religious-historical context to distinguish the proposed explanation from visions and ad hoc supernatural alternatives.

routes.description: Challenge the reliability and interpretation of the claimed historical facts, explain the aftermath through historically accessible developments or natural scenarios, and show that historical method cannot privilege divine bodily resurrection as the best explanation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the factual foundation remains materially underdetermined, historically accessible alternatives remain available, or shared historical criteria cannot assign comparative superiority to the proposed divine-resurrection explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical evidence does not establish Jesus' bodily resurrection as the best historical explanation of what followed the crucifixion.

centralBridges.description: Apply historical source criteria to contest the reliability, independence, consistency, and interpretation of the traditions supporting the proposed core facts.
Show that historical inquiry based on shared probabilistic standards cannot establish unobservable divine action as its preferred conclusion.
Provide historically accessible accounts of burial uncertainty, visions, scriptural reinterpretation, belief development, and narrative growth that reduce the need for bodily resurrection.
Show that the evidence cannot uniquely select the proposed Christian divine explanation over natural scenarios or rival theological interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify literary or theological functions that could account for the Joseph and women traditions without treating their awkwardness as decisive authenticity evidence.
Require a consistent evidential standard across resurrection claims and other ancient miracle reports rather than privileging one inherited tradition.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Evidentiary Standards
sections.rationale: The reliability, independence, dating, transmission, consistency, and appropriate use of the documentary traditions determine how much of the proposed factual foundation is available for any later explanatory inference.

sections.title: Burial and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: The identifiable burial and claimed discovery of an empty tomb supply the principal physical-evidence line for bodily resurrection, while disputes over Joseph, the women, invention, and body removal directly test that line.

sections.title: Appearances and the Origin of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: Reported postmortem experiences and the disciples' resulting convictions require interpretation as bodily encounters, visions, developing scriptural beliefs, or some combination, making this a central causal dispute.

sections.title: Miracle Probability and the Scope of History
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether historical inference may admit divine action and whether antecedent improbability, specific evidence, shared assumptions, and explanatory comparison can make resurrection historically preferable.

sections.title: Competing Explanations, Underdetermination, and Context
sections.rationale: Naturalistic scenarios, developmental accounts, rival supernatural stories, and Jesus' religious-historical context determine whether resurrection uniquely integrates the evidence or remains one interpretation among alternatives.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A historical resurrection case should distinguish the relatively agreed evidentiary facts from the disputed explanation and identify the facts that any adequate explanation must address.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation occurs within Craig's opening statement and introduces his expressly numbered historical case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a clear evidence-versus-explanation framework for organizing the factual foundation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly defines the governing evidentiary and explanatory distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence and explanation is explicit, stable, and readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It acknowledges controversy, though calling the evidence relatively uncontroversial somewhat compresses genuine disputes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is coherent and useful, with only an implicit bridge from scholarly agreement to fact selection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt invokes broad scholarly agreement but does not yet document its representativeness or limits.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally structures the factual-foundation burden and the later comparative explanatory inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move establishes a framework and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig expressly distinguishes relatively agreed evidence from the disputed claim that resurrection best explains it.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus was buried in an identifiable tomb by Joseph of Arimathea, as supported by early independent traditions and the improbability that Christians invented Joseph's role.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels this as his first historical fact and develops it continuously through source and authenticity considerations.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly supplies one of the claimed core historical facts and supporting source warrants.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents a focused factual claim with multiple stated supporting considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burial claim and its main warrants are clear, though source independence remains implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident historical conclusion outruns the compressed defense of independence and invention improbability.

charity.alternative: Joseph's role may be a later literary or apologetic tradition rather than established history.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early attestation can support historicity without proving independence or excluding literary development.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is coherent, though multiple attestation and invention improbability each require bounded supporting bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific traditions are identified, but their independence and the motive-to-invent premise are materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Identifiable burial is an indispensable component of the proposed physical and factual foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers reasons against invention but only briefly engages the strongest source-critical qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig cites early allegedly independent burial traditions and argues that inventing Joseph's role would be unlikely.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Women followers found Jesus' tomb empty on the Sunday after the crucifixion, a conclusion supported by early independent traditions and the awkwardness of inventing women as witnesses.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig announces the second fact and presents a continuous argument from independent attestation and the reported role of women witnesses.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the empty-tomb fact through early-attestation and awkward-witness arguments.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances a core fact and gives two concrete supporting warrants.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empty-tomb proposition is recoverable, but independence and social awkwardness carry implicit scope qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is stronger than the excerpt's abbreviated defense of independence and witness awkwardness.

charity.alternative: Women may serve Mark's literary purposes despite their limited testimonial status in that culture.
charity.decisiveQualification: Literary usefulness weakens but does not eliminate the possible evidential force of an awkward witness tradition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is coherent but depends on unstated assumptions about independence and expected invention practices.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names concrete source features while leaving their independence and cultural generalization underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The claimed empty tomb is an indispensable physical component of the central factual foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument anticipates invention concerns but does not address the strongest literary-function explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig appeals to early independent traditions and the awkwardness of inventing women as the discoverers.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Different individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus alive after his death, as supported by early Pauline testimony, named recipients, group reports, and independent narratives.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly identifies the third fact and develops it through Paul's reported witness list and the Gospel appearance traditions.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly establishes reported experiences that any proposed explanation must address.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides early named and group testimony for a central evidentiary claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: Reports of appearances are clear, but experienced and appeared can range across materially different phenomena.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Early testimony strongly supports experiences, but not without qualification their external or bodily character.

charity.alternative: The reports may concern visionary experiences rather than encounters with a bodily risen Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early and group reports support occurrence claims but do not alone determine the experiences' ontology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference to reported experiences is strong, with a bounded ambiguity between experiences and external appearances.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline testimony, named recipients, groups, and independent narratives provide specific support with an interpretation gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Postmortem experiences are an indispensable central fact requiring explanation under both principal routes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The evidence is presented fairly, though the crucial visionary interpretation remains insufficiently distinguished.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig cites Paul's early list of named and group recipients alongside allegedly independent appearance narratives.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The original disciples sincerely came to believe Jesus had risen despite a crucified messiah and an individual resurrection before the end of history conflicting with their Jewish expectations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this the fourth fact and continuously explains the disciples' prior expectations and the transformation requiring an adequate cause.

response.rationale: This constructive move explains why the disciples' resurrection conviction itself requires a historical account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies contextual expectations that make the belief's emergence explanatorily significant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The central claim is clear, though Jewish expectations are generalized across a diverse historical population.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The contextual contrast has force, but the breadth of Jewish-belief claims needs qualification.

charity.alternative: Scriptural reinterpretation, exaltation belief, and visions could generate resurrection conviction after Jesus' death.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior expectations constrain belief formation without making reinterpretation or development impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contextual inference is coherent, though surprising belief does not by itself establish its proposed cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical contextual claims are relevant but broadly stated and lack representative qualification in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The origin of sincere resurrection belief is a major component of the central explanatory foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move makes the belief surprising but gives limited consideration to gradual reinterpretation mechanisms.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig contrasts the disciples' conviction with expectations concerning a triumphant messiah and general end-time resurrection.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Resurrection best explains the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and origin of belief because it possesses broad explanatory scope and power while proposed naturalistic alternatives lack comparable plausibility.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces his second contention, evaluates resurrection by explanatory criteria, and addresses Ehrman's published miracle objection.

response.rationale: This constructive move expressly advances the motion-level conclusion through comparative explanatory criteria.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the required comparison but substantially compresses its application to rivals.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative proposition and criteria are clear, though the relevant rival set is only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Claiming no better explanation exceeds the excerpt's compressed analysis of naturalistic and theological rivals.

charity.alternative: Different combinations of burial uncertainty, removal, visions, and belief development may explain the evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: A rival need not explain every disputed fact if the factual foundation itself remains uncertain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive form is valid, but criteria are asserted as satisfied without a sufficiently explicit comparative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move largely asserts superior scope, power, and plausibility without representative rival-by-rival demonstration.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly asserts that bodily resurrection best explains the aftermath, exactly contacting the motion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invokes rivals but does not seriously develop their strongest combined or fact-disputing versions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says resurrection passes explanatory power, scope, and plausibility criteria and outperforms naturalistic alternatives.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical conclusions are probabilistic and depend most strongly on numerous contemporary, independent, mutually consistent, and disinterested sources.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman marks this as the beginning of his own case and gives an extended first-person account of historical method and source evaluation.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the standards used to challenge the reliability of the documentary foundation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly enumerates several historically relevant source-quality considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criteria are clear and stable, though their status as preferences rather than absolute requirements is implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic framing appropriately matches the stated source criteria and their comparative evidential role.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed criteria coherently bear on source reliability, with their relative weighting left reasonably implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The criteria are standard and specifically stated, though no defense is given for treating disinterest strongly.

relevanceBurden.rationale: These criteria centrally ground the challenge to reliability, independence, consistency, and interpretation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states methodological criteria without materially presenting or evaluating an opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman lists numerous, contemporary, independent, corroborating, consistent, and disinterested sources as preferable evidence.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The Gospels are late, non-eyewitness, interested accounts transmitted orally for decades and containing material inconsistencies, limiting their reliability as historical sources.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman develops a continuous source-critical argument, identifies the Gospel authorship and transmission problems, and illustrates alleged contradictions.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether the proposed evidentiary facts are sufficiently secure to anchor explanation.
The burial argument depends on early independent and reliable traditions.
The empty-tomb argument depends on early independent and reliable traditions.
The appearance evidence depends partly on the reliability and interpretation of transmitted accounts.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests the dating, eyewitness status, transmission, interests, and consistency of the principal sources.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts several decisive source warrants but does not separately establish how each defect affects every core fact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability challenge is clear, though broad statements about all Gospel accounts need bounded qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited defects limit confidence, but do not without further argument make the accounts generally unreliable.

charity.alternative: Late interested sources can preserve historically reliable traditions and central agreement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Source defects lower confidence without automatically defeating each independently supported central claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-quality critique coherently lowers confidence, with one compressed bridge to general unreliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names specific dating, authorship, transmission, interest, and inconsistency features, though effects vary by claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply centrally attacks the source foundation underlying several indispensable proposed facts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge recognizes relevant evidence but tends to treat cumulative source defects too globally.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman identifies non-eyewitness authorship, late composition, oral transmission, conversion interests, and inconsistencies.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical method identifies what probably occurred, whereas a miracle is by definition the least probable occurrence and therefore cannot be established as historically probable.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman explicitly distinguishes theological from historical claims and sustains a methodological probability argument through the end of his conclusion.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether resurrection may rank as historically probable under historical explanatory criteria.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses a methodological failure: history establishes probability while miracle is defined as least probable, so the conclusion cannot qualify historically.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the central inference and states the claimed defeating methodological consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but miracle and least probable shift between definition and evidential assessment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical boundary is stronger than warranted because specific evidence may affect conditional probability.

charity.alternative: A miracle may have low prior probability yet high posterior probability given sufficiently discriminating evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical method still needs shared means to estimate the divine-action hypothesis and relevant priors.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument risks circularity by defining miracle as least probable and then inferring historical improbability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a methodological rationale but no defended probability rule establishing the categorical exclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the methodological admissibility required for the pro route to reach its conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply identifies a genuine methodological problem but defines away the strongest conditional-probability answer.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues historians establish probable events and that miracles, being least probable, cannot be historically established.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: An intrinsic-improbability objection is incomplete because the conditional probability of resurrection also depends on the specific evidence and the probability of the competing naturalistic explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly identifies Ehrman's position, develops the probability formula, and applies it to the resurrection hypothesis.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether low intrinsic probability alone precludes a probable resurrection conclusion.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the omission of specific evidence and rival likelihoods and states that intrinsic improbability alone cannot decide the posterior comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the probability inference, diagnoses the omitted terms, and states the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional-probability objection is clearly stated and its scope is limited to defeating one incomplete inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It correctly claims that prior or intrinsic improbability alone is insufficient for the posterior comparison.

charity.alternative: The relevant prior could be extremely low and the specific evidence insufficiently discriminating.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing the objection incomplete does not itself show that resurrection has the favorable posterior probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional-probability diagnosis is explicit and valid, while appropriately limited to defeating the stated inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The formal relationship is sound, but the move does not supply defensible numerical or comparative likelihood inputs.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the con route's methodological boundary by exposing an incomplete probability inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately diagnoses the omission while leaving the substantive probability inputs for separate proof.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that posterior probability depends on background information, specific evidence, and naturalistic alternatives.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Imperfections and differences in Gospel details do not defeat the four core facts because ancient sources need not meet ideal standards, and the accounts retain agreement on the central sequence.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig expressly returns to his first contention and answers Ehrman's objections concerning source quality and inconsistencies.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether Gospel imperfections and inconsistencies defeat the reliability of the core facts.
Ideal source criteria must be applied realistically to ancient evidence rather than as absolute prerequisites.

response.rationale: The reply argues that ancient sources need not be perfect and that central narrative agreement survives differences in detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the reliability demand but only partially answers authorship, transmission, independence, and interest concerns.

precisionFindings.rationale: Central agreement is intelligible, though the boundary between central facts and disputed details is partly contestable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Central agreement has evidential force, but it does not fully neutralize dependence and transmission concerns.

charity.alternative: Agreement may result from literary dependence or shared tradition rather than independent confirmation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Central agreement supports preservation but has less force if the accounts are not independent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between central agreement and detail differences is coherent, with independence left underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies central agreement and an opposing concession but compresses documentation and source-dependence analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary source-defense bridge without independently completing the factual foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly addresses inconsistency but underaddresses the strongest dependence and transmission qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that imperfections are expected in ancient sources and that the accounts agree on the central sequence.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Paul does not attest burial by Joseph of Arimathea, and treating sparse early traditions as historical while discounting embellished later accounts applies an inconsistent source standard.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman identifies this as his second criticism and directly examines Craig's treatment of Paul and later Gospel traditions.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether early independent evidence specifically attests burial by Joseph of Arimathea.
The reply asks whether later embellished details are historical under the proposed central-agreement standard.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes Pauline attestation to Joseph and exposes tension in selectively using early and later traditions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central attestation warrant but does not fully analyze all alleged independent burial sources.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited claim about Paul's silence and the consistency challenge are both clear and properly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately limits itself to weakening attestation and exposing a source-standard inconsistency.

charity.alternative: Paul's burial reference may preserve the underlying tradition without naming Joseph.
charity.decisiveQualification: Generic burial attestation supports burial but does not independently attest Joseph's identity or tomb ownership.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between attesting burial and attesting Joseph is explicit and inferentially important.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's omission is concrete evidence, though argument from silence cannot by itself disprove the Joseph tradition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply centrally attacks a key element of the claimed burial and factual foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the distinction between generic burial and the more specific Joseph tradition.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman distinguishes Paul's generic burial reference from attestation to Joseph and questions selective source treatment.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The women-at-the-tomb and Joseph traditions could have been invented because both serve Mark's literary and theological purposes, so their alleged awkwardness does not establish historicity.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman presents the third criticism and analyzes Mark's narrative themes to explain the disputed traditions' possible invention.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether inventing women as witnesses would have been too awkward to serve Christian purposes.
The Joseph tradition is also defended by an asserted lack of plausible Christian invention motive.

response.rationale: The reply supplies literary and theological functions for both traditions, directly challenging the awkwardness warrants.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts both invention-improbability claims, though it does not establish that invention occurred.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modal conclusion is carefully stated as a possible literary explanation rather than proof of invention.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The possibility claim matches the literary-function evidence and appropriately avoids claiming demonstrated invention.

charity.alternative: An awkward tradition can be literary useful and nevertheless derive from historical memory.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing a motive for invention defeats decisiveness, not the remaining positive case for historicity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A plausible literary function directly defeats the inference from no imaginable motive to likely authenticity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The functions are concrete and relevant, though their presence does not independently verify compositional invention.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary burden concerning literary and theological invention motives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately limits its consequence to undermining the argument from alleged lack of motive.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues that the women and Joseph traditions fit Mark's literary and theological agenda.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Ancient postmortem appearances did not require a reanimated physical body, so reports of appearances do not by themselves establish bodily resurrection or divine action.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman marks this as his fourth criticism and sustains it through ancient examples before restating the methodological conclusion.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether appearance reports specifically support a bodily resurrection rather than visions.
The comparative inference requires connecting appearance evidence to the proposed bodily and divine explanation.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes postmortem appearance from bodily reanimation and challenges the historical status of supernatural body claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the interpretive bridge from appearances to bodily resurrection, with a clear alternative category.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between appearance reports and bodily reanimation is explicit, stable, and appropriately limited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Appearance reports do not entail reanimation, though saying historians are unable to establish it is stronger.

charity.alternative: Some appearance traditions contain embodied interaction rather than merely visionary experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Embodied narrative details may be later or theological and require independent historical defense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The non-entailment from appearances to bodily reanimation is clear and directly undermines an overstrong inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well supported, but the historical prevalence and interpretation claims remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the interpretation of an indispensable appearance component of the factual foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly identifies the bodily alternative while preserving the need to warrant its historical details.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman distinguishes ancient postmortem appearances from reanimation and treats extraordinary body properties as theological claims.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Lack of direct access to God does not bar an inference to resurrection because science and history routinely infer inaccessible entities and past events from presently available evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Craig's direct response to Ehrman's methodological objection and uses Craig's first-person framing throughout.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether historical inquiry may infer a cause that is not directly observable.
The reply also challenges the claim that lack of direct access bars historical inference to resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply invokes ordinary inference from present traces to inaccessible entities and past events as a methodological analogy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the access objection but only partially answers probability, agency, and shared-standard concerns.

precisionFindings.rationale: Inaccessibility is clear, but the analogy groups past natural events and divine agency under a broad term.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It correctly defeats a direct-access requirement but overextends the analogy toward methodological admissibility generally.

charity.alternative: Inferring an inaccessible ordinary cause differs from inferring intentional supernatural agency with uncertain priors.
charity.decisiveQualification: Inaccessibility alone is no bar, but comparability and probability still require separate warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy validly rebuts direct-access necessity but does not establish parity between all inaccessible causes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples from science and history support indirect inference, while the divine-agency extension remains underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports methodological admissibility by rebutting a claimed bar to inaccessible causes.

representationalCharity.rationale: The analogy catches one weakness while insufficiently preserving the strongest methodological distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig compares resurrection inference with scientific and historical inferences from present evidence to inaccessible objects or events.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Treating divine resurrection as a historical explanation presupposes theistic belief and cannot produce conclusions shared by historians across divergent theological perspectives.
moves.attributionBasis: A clear new Ehrman turn addresses Craig by name and contrasts theological belief with the shared canons of historical research.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether indirect inference suffices when the proposed cause presupposes disputed theology.
Conditional comparison requires priors and likelihoods that historians of divergent worldviews can share.

response.rationale: The reply argues that historical canons seek conclusions available across theological perspectives and that divine resurrection lacks that shared basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts methodological admissibility, though it does not prove consensus is required for every inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The shared-standards demand is clear, but sameness of conclusions is stated more broadly than methodological practice warrants.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Shared public standards are important, though universal cross-worldview agreement is too demanding as stated.

charity.alternative: Shared evidence can support an inference even when historians disagree because of different background probabilities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Disagreement does not invalidate inference, but disputed theological priors weaken claims of public historical establishment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The public-standard concern is coherent, with one overstrong bridge from shared method to shared conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The pluralism example supports the methodological concern but does not establish a strict disciplinary prohibition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the con methodological-boundary burden concerning shared probabilistic standards.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures the public-method issue while somewhat overstating the requirement of identical conclusions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues that historical methods must remain usable by historians across divergent theological commitments.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: An ordinary body-removal scenario followed by visions remains historically more plausible than divine resurrection when the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and martyrdom claims are disputed.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman opens his concluding turn, identifies Craig's claims explicitly, and replies point by point to the asserted facts and body-removal objections.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether resurrection explains the aftermath better than available ordinary alternatives.
The alternative disputes whether Joseph's identifiable burial is historically established.
The alternative disputes whether an empty tomb is independently established.
The alternative interprets appearances as visions rather than bodily encounters.

response.rationale: The reply combines factual uncertainty, possible body removal, and visions to challenge resurrection's claimed comparative superiority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the comparative demand and several facts, but the combined scenario remains only lightly developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternative is clearly modal and appropriately conditioned on disputes concerning the asserted core facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The ordinary components are possible, though their combination and comparative likelihood are not fully warranted.

charity.alternative: Resurrection offers a unified explanation where removal plus visions requires multiple independent suppositions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Unity matters only after the facts and the probabilities of each component are adequately established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scenario is possible and relevant, but its components are combined without a developed causal sequence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The factual disputes are specified, while removal and vision likelihoods receive limited affirmative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that resurrection is not established as the best explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the unified rival but does not fully answer the concern that its own account is conjunctive.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman disputes burial and empty-tomb claims and proposes ordinary removal plus visionary experiences as more plausible.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Resurrection belief can develop through scriptural reinterpretation of Jesus' death, belief in his exaltation, subsequent visions, circulating stories, and eventual Gospel narratives.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman explicitly introduces what he thinks occurred and presents a continuous causal account through the emergence of later written narratives.

components.text: The decisive demand is how sincere resurrection belief could arise despite contrary prior expectations.
The account interprets later experiences as visions shaped by an already developing exaltation belief.

response.rationale: The reply supplies a staged causal account involving scripture, exaltation, circulating stories, visions, and narrative development.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the belief-origin demand with a causal sequence, though its chronology is speculative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The developmental scenario and its modal status are clear, with uncertainty about timing expressly acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The scenario is possible and intelligible, but specific timing and causal order remain weakly evidenced.

charity.alternative: Very early creedal material and sincere eyewitness claims constrain a long or late developmental process.
charity.decisiveQualification: Early belief limits the timeline without determining whether the initiating experiences were bodily encounters.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal sequence is coherent, though some ordering assumptions and feedback between belief and visions are implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Known mechanisms are identified, but the proposed timing and sequence are substantially speculative in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supplies an accessible alternative-development account for resurrection belief and appearances.

representationalCharity.rationale: The account addresses rapid belief formation only incompletely and permits an overly elastic timeline.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman proposes scriptural reinterpretation, exaltation belief, story circulation, visions, and eventual Gospel development.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical evidence cannot select the Christian divine-resurrection account over rival supernatural stories because the competing accounts are theological interpretations judged by theological criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman answers the audience question in a sustained first-person response and contrasts theological legitimacy with historical evaluation.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether historical criteria uniquely prefer the Christian divine-resurrection explanation.
Indirect inference alone does not supply criteria for selecting among rival supernatural agents or purposes.

response.rationale: The reply argues that rival supernatural accounts are adjudicated through theological rather than shared historical criteria.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts uniqueness and comparative selection, though it does not analyze particular historical discriminators.

precisionFindings.rationale: The underdetermination claim and distinction between historical evidence and theological interpretation are clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence underdetermines divine agency, though categorical exclusion of historical comparison is too strong.

charity.alternative: Context, prior claims, and explanatory fit may discriminate among rival supernatural interpretations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such contextual evidence can compare stories without independently validating supernatural agency or intention.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from multiple compatible theological causes to underdetermination is coherent and materially relevant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological distinction is supported conceptually, though no representative rival set is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the burden that evidence cannot uniquely select the proposed Christian divine explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move captures underdetermination but underplays the possible evidential relevance of religious-historical context.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues that supernatural alternatives are theological interpretations evaluated by theological rather than historical criteria.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Rival theological explanations can be compared by explanatory criteria, and resurrection is less ad hoc and more plausible when interpreted within Jesus' claims and Israelite religious-historical context.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig begins the immediate counter-response and applies his stated explanatory criteria to Ehrman's hypothetical rival account.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether rival theological explanations can be comparatively assessed rather than declared historically tied.
The reply proposes explanatory criteria and context as publicly discussable comparative considerations.

response.rationale: The reply argues that ad hocness, plausibility, and Jesus' religious-historical context can discriminate among theological rivals.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts comparative underdetermination but does not fully specify or independently defend the contextual evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is clear, though the relevant religious-historical context is left materially compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling resurrection extremely plausible exceeds the brief contextual and comparative support supplied here.

charity.alternative: Context may distinguish narratives while still failing to identify which supernatural agent acted.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative fit reduces underdetermination only if the contextual claims and rival priors are independently warranted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Context and ad hocness can discriminate among hypotheses, but the decisive comparative bridge remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply relies heavily on asserted implausibility and an undeveloped religious-historical context.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks theological underdetermination and supports comparative and contextual pro-route bridges.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the strongest problem but asserts contextual superiority without adequately developing its qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig appeals to ad hocness, plausibility, Jesus' claims, and Israelite context to compare theological hypotheses.
